analysis.one_liner: Makes pharmacy benefit managers legal fiduciaries for employer health plans and requires fee disclosure.
analysis.headline: Introduced in the House on December 18, 2025 and referred to the Education and Workforce Committee; no committee action or vote has taken place.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would write pharmacy benefit managers (PBMs) — the middlemen who build drug networks, decide which drugs get covered, and negotiate manufacturer rebates for employer health plans — into federal pension law as fiduciaries. That would legally obligate them to act solely in the interest of workers and their families, not their own profits. It would also require PBMs and pharmacy claims processors to disclose every form of compensation they receive, including hidden rebate and network deals, and would bar them from using contracts to escape liability if they breach that duty.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers, retirees, and family members covered by employer-sponsored health plans, who would gain a legal tool to sue PBMs over hidden fees and self-interested drug coverage decisions, and employers who sponsor those plans and could see more of their drug spending reach actual prescription costs.

how_it_helps.text: The bill adds PBMs to the definition of an ERISA fiduciary for any employer group health plan, whenever a PBM builds a drug network or formulary, negotiates or aggregates manufacturer rebates, processes and pays drug claims, or performs utilization review — meaning they would owe a legal duty of loyalty and care to the plan and its members.

It expands the required fee disclosures so that PBMs and third-party administrators must disclose direct and indirect compensation, including compensation earned through maintaining drug networks and formularies and purchasing drugs from manufacturers, wholesalers, rebate aggregators, or group purchasing organizations.

It bars PBMs from being indemnified or otherwise relieved from liability for fiduciary breaches, and voids any contract provision that tries to do so, so PBMs cannot shift the cost of their own wrongdoing to employers.

The fiduciary and disclosure rules take effect for plan years beginning at least 12 months after enactment, and the bill also clarifies a PBM cannot be the 'responsible plan fiduciary' for the disclosure process except for its own employee plan.

analysis.who_pays: PBMs and the large companies that own them — CVS (Caremark), Cigna (Express Scripts), and UnitedHealth (Optum Rx) — which would lose the ability to keep rebate and fee arrangements undisclosed and would face fiduciary-breach lawsuits; some added compliance costs could also flow to employers.
analysis.who_pays_short: PBM middlemen and their corporate parents

drawbacks.text: The bill covers only ERISA employer group health plans, so PBMs would remain outside this fiduciary standard for Medicare Part D, Medicaid, and individually purchased insurance plans — a large share of the drug market [S2].

It does not cap drug prices or ban specific PBM practices like spread pricing; it relies on disclosure and litigation to change behavior, so results would depend on plan sponsors and members actually enforcing their new rights, and compliance costs could eventually be passed through to employers and premiums [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the tens of millions of people on employer insurance, the benefit is real: a fiduciary standard with teeth (no indemnification, mandatory fee transparency) directly targets the opacity that lets PBMs keep rebates and fees away from employers and members. The main honest caveats are that it leaves the Medicare and individual markets untouched and enforcement depends on private lawsuits rather than direct price limits.

outcome.mechanism: It was just introduced and referred to the House Education and Workforce Committee, where it is waiting for the committee to act.

narrative.text: Representative Jake Auchincloss introduced H.R. 6837 in the House on December 18, 2025, joined by Representative Mackenzie as cosponsor.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Education and Workforce on the day it was introduced.
No committee markup, floor vote, or further action has been recorded since the referral.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far no one; the status quo continues, which favors the PBMs, who operate without a fiduciary duty to health plans.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The status quo — the PBM industry

for.name: Rep. Jake Auchincloss
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to make PBMs fiduciaries under ERISA and referred it to the Education and Workforce Committee.

for.name: Rep. Ryan Mackenzie
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it bipartisan sponsorship.

sides.party_line_note: Too early to tell: the bill has bipartisan sponsorship — one Democrat who introduced it and one Republican cosponsor — and no votes have been held.

industries.industry: Pharmacy benefit managers (Optum Rx, Express Scripts, CVS Caremark)
industries.note: The bill makes PBMs fiduciaries for employer plans, forces disclosure of rebate and network compensation, and blocks indemnification, exposing their fee and rebate model to lawsuits. PBMs profit from arrangements employers and members cannot see, which puts their interest against the bill's transparency requirements.

industries.industry: Health insurers with PBM subsidiaries (UnitedHealth, Cigna, CVS/Aetna)
industries.note: Most large insurers own the biggest PBMs, so disclosure and fiduciary liability hits their vertically integrated drug businesses. Insurers keep their role in employer plans but lose revenue opacity in the drug benefit.
Employers buying health plans would finally see PBM compensation and could sue over self-dealing, though they may absorb some compliance and potential fee changes.
Fiduciary pressure on PBM reimbursement and network practices could modestly improve pharmacy reimbursement rates, though the bill does not address pharmacy payment directly.

analysis.trajectory: Bills introduced this late with a single cosponsor rarely reach the floor, and the House Education and Workforce Committee has taken no action. However, PBM reform has drawn bipartisan attention in both chambers, so some version of fiduciary or disclosure legislation could move — most likely folded into a broader health or retirement package rather than advancing as this standalone bill.
